question: What is the main focus of the study of embryology?
explanation: You've got this! Embryology simply tracks how a human grows and changes from a single cell all the way until birth. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is knowing embryology useful for nurses working in antenatal clinics?

options.A: It replaces the need for routine ultrasound scans in pregnancy
options.B: It allows nurses to perform surgical corrections of the heart
options.C: It dictates the exact dietary requirements for the mother
options.D: It helps identify developmental milestones and birth defects early

explanation: Great nursing insight here! When you understand normal growth timelines, you can easily spot early warning signs and give great guidance to expectant mothers. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the final chromosomal state of a mature human gamete (sperm or egg)?
explanation: Remember that gametes carry half the normal number of chromosomes (haploid). That way, when sperm and egg meet, they restore the full (diploid) number! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: Spermatogenesis produces four functional sperm cells, but oogenesis produces only one mature egg. Why does this happen?

options.A: Oocytes undergo mitosis instead of meiosis during development
options.B: Unequal cytoplasmic division saves nutrients for one large egg
options.C: Primary spermatocytes degenerate before completing the second division
options.D: Sperm cells require more mitochondria to swim long distances

explanation: Think of it as nature pooling all its resources! Oogenesis packs most of the cytoplasm and nutrients into a single egg so it has the best chance to survive after fertilization. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: Where does fertilization of the human egg normally take place?
explanation: The ampulla is the wider middle section of the fallopian tube, and it's the favorite meeting spot for the traveling sperm and the released egg! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the main job of the cortical reaction right after a sperm enters the egg?

options.A: Preventing fertilization by more than one sperm
options.B: Releasing digestive enzymes from the sperm head
options.C: Triggering the immediate first mitotic cell division
options.D: Initiating the production of progesterone hormones

explanation: Once the first sperm gets in, the egg puts up a quick chemical shield (the cortical reaction) to lock the door against any extra sperm. Clever design! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: What do we call the solid, grape-like cluster of cells formed a few days after fertilization?
explanation: The word 'morula' comes from the Latin for mulberry because this tight little ball of cells looks just like one! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: Inside the developing blastocyst, which part goes on to form the actual embryo?
explanation: You guessed it—the inner cell mass (or embryoblast) groups together to build the actual tissues of the baby, while the outer cells build the support systems. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which hormone, produced by the early placenta tissue, keeps the corpus luteum working in early pregnancy?
explanation: That's hCG—the famous hormone pregnancy tests look for! It tells the ovary to keep producing progesterone until the placenta is fully ready to take over. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary role of the trophoblast cells during early pregnancy?

options.A: Production of red blood cells for the embryo
options.B: Invasive attachment and formation of the placenta
options.C: Providing all the locomotion for the moving zygote
options.D: Direct formation of the central nervous system

explanation: The trophoblast cells are the pioneers! They burrow into the uterine lining to help plant the blastocyst securely and build the placenta. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which structure marks the official start of gastrulation on the embryo?
explanation: The primitive streak shows up like a tiny groove, helping map out the baby's left/right and head/tail sides before the three main germ layers form. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: A birth defect linked to the embryonic endoderm would most likely affect which body system?
explanation: Think of the endoderm as the inner lining layer—it mainly builds the inner tubes of your body, like the digestive and respiratory tracts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: The neural tube develops from the folding of which primary germ layer?
explanation: The ectoderm is the outermost layer. It thickens and rolls up into a tube to form the brain and spinal cord—our control center! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: Why do midwives and doctors eagerly advise pregnant women to take early folic acid supplements?
explanation: Folic acid is a super-nutrient in early pregnancy! It helps the neural tube close properly, preventing serious conditions like spina bifida. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: During which phase of pregnancy is the developing embryo most sensitive to harmful substances (teratogens)?
explanation: The first trimester is when all the major organs are first sketching themselves out, making the tiny embryo extra sensitive to outside toxins or infections. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a harmful teratogen during early pregnancy?
explanation: Good food and proper nutrition help a baby grow strong! Medications, infections, and radiation are the ones we watch out for as harmful teratogens. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)
